sentences.text: Grandma's dishes won't survive a storage unit, and the unit costs more monthly than they're worth anyway. Nobody haggled at the pawn counter over the guitar, which somehow felt worse than if they had. Overtime used to be a choice; now I take every shift posted and it still doesn't touch the arrears. Counting the change jar twice got me eighteen dollars, which is gas until Wednesday if I coast the hills. Called my sister at lunch; her silence cost me more than the rent I was asking about. A thumbs-up from my cousin about borrowing his truck; that tiny icon is holding the whole moving day together. Some nights I lay the bills out across the table like a hand of cards nobody would bet on. Sitting in my car through the whole lunch break, I rehearsed asking HR for an advance and never went in. Rent, then electric, then the minimum on the card — some sequence of those three, never all of them. Somebody at work joked about vacation plans and I laughed with a mouth full of vending-machine crackers. Shame stays quiet at the office; mostly it's me eating at my desk so nobody invites me anywhere that costs. Forty-one dollars after the phone bill clears — that's the whole month, sitting in one number. Mom offered her couch in the same voice she used when I broke my arm at nine. Taped at eye level, the notice on the door sat where every neighbor could read the amount. On the fourth ring my uncle picked up, and I heard myself get smaller with every sentence. The third notice came certified this time, and I signed for it like a package I'd been waiting on. I keep the moving boxes flat in the closet so my daughter won't ask what they're for. Do I pack the books or sell them? The bookshelf itself already has a buyer. The editor requested that page fourteen end mid-gesture, so the turn lands on the empty apartment splash. Panel three repeats panel one exactly, except the coffee has gone cold and her phone screen is dark. I want to write a suicide letter.
